summary:
The week of September 21-28, 2026 marked the sharpest escalation yet in statewide action on data centers, coming simultaneously from both parties' flagship states. On September 21, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a seven-bill package — SB 1168, SB 886, SB 887, AB 1577, AB 2383, AB 2469 and AB 2619 — that his office calls the most comprehensive data center laws in the nation, directing the CPUC to make data centers pay for the grid upgrades their load requires, creating a separate electricity rate class for them, and adding environmental review and water and land-use requirements. The same day, Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt all data center permits statewide — including environmental permits and even fully 'islanded' facilities running on behind-the-meter generation — until ERCOT completes its grid audit, expected in mid-December. Together with Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey's September 8 executive order conditioning state permits for facilities over 25 MW on local approval and community benefits agreements, three of the country's largest economies now impose statewide restrictions by law or executive action.
Local restrictions continued at an unrelenting pace, with roughly two dozen jurisdictions acting in a single week. Permanent bans arrived in Wakulla County, Florida, Raritan Township, New Jersey, and Calexico, California (the state's third municipal ban). New or extended moratoriums passed in Baltimore County, Maryland (through the end of 2027); Spartanburg and Kershaw counties in South Carolina; North Port and Marion County in Florida; Fayette County, Ohio; Zionsville and Owen County in Indiana; Normal, Illinois (through May 31, 2027); Marshall County, Iowa; North Mankato and Woodbury, Minnesota; Tulare County, California (a 10-month extension); Pima County, Arizona (120 days); and Salem, Oregon (120 days with a task force). The wave is also reaching major cities: an Oakland council committee advanced a 45-day pause toward an October 6 vote, Buffalo's two-year moratorium heads to a possible unanimous vote on September 29, and Boston is weighing a citywide ban.
The most consequential single local vote came in Virginia, where Prince William County — one of the largest data center markets in the world — voted 8-0 on September 22 to end by-right data center development countywide, requiring Special Use Permits outside a sharply shrunken overlay district. But the week also showed the limits and friction of the movement: Pulaski County, Arkansas passed sweeping data center regulations 11-4 only to see County Judge Barry Hyde veto them two days later (an override vote is possible October 27); Raton, New Mexico rejected a proposed moratorium 3-2 despite a 477-signature petition; and Spartanburg County's 5-1 final passage was immediately muddied by a disputed, unposted 'reconsideration' meeting that a press association attorney called illegal. New Jersey regulators separately levied the largest data center enforcement action in state history — a $1.07 million fine against a Vineland facility running 62 generators without air permits.
Trends to watch: whether California's package becomes a template for other legislatures convening in January; whether Texas's permitting freeze holds through the ERCOT audit and how it affects the roughly 200 GW of requested interconnection; the October 6 Loudoun County debate on ending by-right permitting, which would extend the Prince William model to the heart of Data Center Alley; pending votes in Buffalo (September 29), Oakland (October 6), Fort Wayne (October 13), and Leon County, Florida (October 13); and the Pulaski County veto override fight in late October. With more than 300 local moratoriums and bans now adopted nationwide and polling showing data center siting a liability in the 2026 midterms, restriction — not incentive — is now the default posture of local government toward new data center development.
